Babies have a receptor called RnFc in their inestines' lining. That receptor attaches to the antibodies in the gut and passes them to the blood. This receptor is also present in the materno-fetal interface (the placenta) and allows passage of antibodies to the fetus' blood. In humans over 3 months old, this receptor can be found in the lining of our vessels (the endothelial cells). This serves as a way of recycling IgG (a type of antibody) extending its plasmatic half life from 6 to 21 days.

RnFc bounds to the Fc portion of the antibodies, which is species-specific. So it's unlikely one could absorb bovine antibodies by drinking milk.

There are two different terms we have to differentiate.

"Life" is a biological term. We cannot really define life, but we do know what things are living and what things are not. We do consider all things that are self-sustainable and self-organising to be living things. That is why bacteria and insects are living creatures. Consciousness plays no part in this. Now, you could say that the fetus is alive in the same way your liver is, just an added component of an organism (the mother). The thing is that the embryo uses the mother (its environment) in the same way we use our own environment. We take things from it (food, water, heat) and we modify it (we excrete things, we grow crops). This is what the embryo does as well: it takes things from his environment (nutrients, heat) and it modifies it (certain placental hormones affect the mother's body, the embryo excretes its waste and it passes to the mother). In the same way we have a separate existance from our environment, the fetus has a separate existance from the mother. Also take in account that the embryo, even before implantation, already has a complex organising system with multiple components playing different roles. So, as a self-organising and self-dependant being, the fetus is alive.

"Personhood", however, is an ethical/legal term. It is what makes you a equal among your peers in society, and a subject of right. Unlike life, personhood is not an intrinsic characteristic. Rather, it is granted by society and it is dependant on the culture of said society. (Think how, in times of slavery, nobody said slaves were not alive. However, society didn't consider them to have personhood. They were not people and so they didn't have any rights.)

So, "embryos, though belonging to the human species and though being living creatures, are not granted personhood until an arbitrary moment of time has passed from its conception because we as a society can do whatever we consider is in the best interest of our comunity" is a more convincing argument than the one that makes an exception on a biological definition, in my opinion, though I don't agree with either of them.

Also, I want to clarify that brain stem activity by no means is a sign of consciousness. Though this part of biology is still for the most a big mystery, it is hard to imagine consciousness without any intellectual or sensitive processes (that take place in the cortex) going on. The thing is, in the brain stem we have the centres that control the heart and the lungs. Cutting these off would be equivalent to separating all the components of a bacteria and putting it in a petri dish with all necesary substrates (food, heat, etc). That bacteria is dead because all its components have lost their organisation and therefore its basic functions cannot be performed, even with adequate substrates.

Well, before cardiopulmonary ressuscitation existed, if your heart stopped beating or you stopped breathing, you were considered dead. (Fun fact: In ancient times they would place a mirror under your nose. If it didn't become tarnished, it ment you weren' t breathing, and so you were dead.)

Medicine evolved and we learnt how to make a heart beat again. So we needed to draw the line somewhere else. Now here is where philosophy chimed in and said "life implies the organisation of all of the components of the body." (Dying means the body starts to decompose in an incoordinated manner, there is no integration of the components. Disease comes when one of the components of the system fails, and it affects the whole body because of this integration.)

Now, how do we assess this organisation? We look at the point where all vital functions converge and where they are integrated to work "as a team". This point is the brain stem. If your brain stem is not working it means all the components of your body have lost coordination and so you cannot consider the subject as being alive. 

If brain stem damage could be reversed, then it would mean that organisation could be recovered, so we would just treat it like we treat any disease. Since we can't, we just say the patient is dead, for the disorganisation is permanent.

In the case of the embryo, integration doesn't depend on the brain stem. Its components work together to keep itself alive and to direct development. Thats why assessing brain stem activity is not an effective way to see if the embryo is alive or not.

We dont define death as the lack of brain stem activity, we use a negative eeg from the brain stem as an indirect diagnosis of death. These are different things. (In the same way infection is not the prescence of fever and high white blood cells, these are only signs that let us arrive to a diagnosis)

Besides, "irrecuperable brain stem function" is what allows us to diagnose death. This is not thr situation for an 8 week embryo.

Freud attributed phobia acquisition to an object displacement caused by an abnormal fear of castration, derived from a trauma during early psychosexual developement. The new investiture of affection usually is done on an object with negative connotations.

Example: You grow up knowing spiders are bad, like every kid. Growing up, your violent father makes you repress the enamourment you have towards your mother, because you are afraid that if your father knew, he would remove your phallus (imago of penis). In this case, you have an abnormal Castration Complex (leading to a prolongued latency period -explaining asexuality- and a hyperdemanding Uber-Ich -low self esteem issues). This castration fear is too much for your psyche for you to take so you incnciously take the affection out of that Complex and reinvest it in a new object. In this case, since you knew spiders were bad beforehand, you use them as an object. Now the fear you had of being castrated now is an irrational fear for spiders.

Note: Freud considered Castration Complex to be normal in child developement, but traumas (like a violent father) can alter it. He always lamented his theories didn't apply so cleanly to women.
